name: Abhyanga oil massage

card.summary: A traditional Ayurvedic warm-oil massage of the whole body, done as a daily self-massage or by a therapist, used for soft, moisturised skin, relaxation and an overall glow.
card.aka: Abhyanga; Ayurvedic oil massage; Nitya-Abhyanga (daily self-massage)
card.note: Oils can stain towels and clog drains and some people react to specific oils or herbs; people with skin conditions may wish to check with a clinician.

quick.overview:
Abhyanga is an Ayurvedic practice in which warm, often herb-infused oil is massaged over the whole body, and it is described in the tradition as part of the daily routine (dinacharya). People use it for softer, better moisturised skin and hair, a relaxed feel, and the healthy look that comes with them.

Research is small. A pilot study of 20 healthy adults found that a one-hour abhyanga session reduced subjective stress and heart rate, and a 2026 randomized trial tested daily self-massage alongside stretching in students. Direct studies of skin appearance are not listed here.
quick.how: Typically sesame oil is warmed and massaged over the body in long strokes on the limbs and circles at the joints, either by a therapist or as a daily self-massage, and is often followed by a warm bath or steam. Oils may be chosen to suit a person's Ayurvedic dosha type or season.
quick.risks: Oils can cause irritation or allergic reactions in some people, and oily floors and tubs are a slip risk. Ayurveda as a medical system is described as pseudoscientific by some reviewers, and abhyanga's traditional claims about doshas and toxins are not verified in trials.

lead: Abhyanga is an Ayurvedic oil massage in which warm, dosha-specific, herb-infused oil is applied over the entire body. It can be a stand-alone therapy, a pre-treatment step in Panchakarma, or a self-massage done by the person themselves, and is often followed by steam or a warm bath [1][2].

For appearance, proponents say it improves dry hair and flaky skin and gives a lustrous complexion [1][3]. The chain is moisturising oil on the skin, softer and more even-looking skin, plus relaxation that people associate with a rested look.

Clinical research is limited. A pilot study with 20 healthy adults reported lower subjective stress and heart rate after a one-hour session [4], and a randomized trial examined daily self-massage alongside stretching for hamstring flexibility [5]. Ayurveda as a whole is described by Wikipedia as pseudoscientific [6].

chain: Warm oil is massaged over skin and scalp
Skin feels softer and less dry-looking
Relaxation and a healthier-looking glow, as practitioners describe
angle.text: Practitioners describe abhyanga as improving dry skin and hair and giving a lustrous complexion. Studies of the practice have measured stress and flexibility rather than skin appearance.

paras: Wikipedia describes abhyanga as a massage with warm oil, tailored to the person's dosha type, with sesame as the traditional base. It may be followed by svedana (steam therapy) or a warm bath, and can be done alone or by one or more therapists [1]. In Ayurvedic theory, oil massage together with sweating therapies is believed to open the body's channels [6].
Abhyanga is listed as part of the daily routine dinacharya in classical Ayurvedic texts and is described in Grokipedia as extending from scalp to soles of the feet [1][3].

Proponents say it supports joint health, nourishes the body's tissues, rebalances the doshas, relieves dry hair and flaky skin, and promotes deep relaxation [1]. Other descriptions add sleep quality and a lustrous complexion [3].

A pilot study of 10 women and 10 men gave a one-hour abhyanga session and found large reductions in subjective stress and in heart rate, with a blood-pressure drop only in a prehypertensive subgroup [4]. A randomized trial of 42 male college students compared daily self-massage plus stretching with stretching alone over four weeks, measuring hamstring extensibility, stiffness and stretch tolerance [5]. Abhyanga was also one component of a combined Ayurvedic programme in a 10-patient study of balance in cerebellar ataxia [7]. Reviews of Ayurvedic stress management and insomnia treatments discuss oil therapies among other methods [8][9]. No trial listed here measured skin or hair appearance.

Wikipedia's Ayurveda article describes the tradition's theory and practice as pseudoscientific, notes that critics regard the doshas as fictional concepts, and warns about metal-containing preparations, which concern oral rasashastra remedies [6]. Wikipedia's abhyanga article flags that its claims lack cited clinical studies [1].
